                    ### Question
                    A 24-year-old man presents to the postoperative unit after undergoing an appendectomy following 2 episodes of acute appendicitis. He complains of nausea and vomiting. On physical examination, his temperature is 36.9°C (98.4ºF), pulse rate is 96/minute, blood pressure is 122/80 mm Hg, and respiratory rate is 14/minute. His abdomen is soft on palpation, and bowel sounds are normoactive. Intravenous ondansetron is administered, and the patient reports relief from his symptoms. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of action of this drug?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Inhibition of gastroesophageal motility
opb. Inhibition of dopamine receptors on chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ)
opc. Stimulation of 5-HT3 receptors on the nucleus of the tractus solitarius
opd. Stimulation of intestinal and colonic motility
ope. Inhibition of serotonin receptors on the vagal and spinal afferent nerves from the intestines

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
Ondansetron is a selective 5-HT3 receptor antagonist, primarily acting on the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) and vagal afferent nerves. The mechanism of action involves binding to 5-HT3 receptors, leading to inhibition of serotonin signaling, which reduces the stimulation of the vomiting center and alleviates nausea and vomiting. The reasoning chains that correctly describe this mechanism include the inhibition of serotonin receptors on vagal afferents and the blocking of serotonin receptors in the CTZ. The option that best explains the mechanism of action of ondansetron is 'Inhibition of serotonin receptors on the vagal and spinal afferent nerves from the intestines,' as it aligns with the consensus on ondansetron's pharmacological effects.
